{{Short description|Treaty between First Nations and Canadian governments}}
The '''Nisgaʼa Final Agreement''', also known as the '''Nisgaʼa Treaty''', is a treaty that was settled between the [[Nisgaʼa|Nisg̱aʼa]], the government of [[British Columbia]], and the [[Government of Canada]]. It was signed on 27 May 1998 and came into effect on 11 May 2000.<ref name="nisga-a-lisims_2000">{{cite web |url=https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/environment/natural-resource-stewardship/consulting-with-first-nations/first-nations-negotiations/first-nations-a-z-listing/nisga-a-lisims-government |title=Nisgaʼa Lisims Government |work=Government of British Columbia |date=nd |access-date=24 October 2017}}</ref> As part of the settlement, nearly {{convert|2,000|km2|sqmi|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} of land in the [[Nass River]] valley was officially recognized as Nisg̱a'a,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nisgaalisims.ca/our-land |title=Our Land |publisher=Nisga’a Lisims Government |location=[[New Aiyansh, British Columbia]] |date=nd |access-date=24 October 2017}}</ref> and a {{convert|300,000|dam3|cuft}} (approx.&nbsp;240,000 acre-feet) water reservation was also created. [[Bear Glacier Provincial Park]] was also created as a result of this agreement. Thirty-one Nisgaʼa placenames in the territory became official names.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www2.gov.bc.ca/assets/gov/british-columbians-our-governments/our-history/historic-places/documents/heritage/showcasenisgaa.pdf |title=Map of Nisgaʼa Lands and Treaty Placenames |work=Government of British Columbia |date=nd |access-date=24 October 2017}}</ref>  The land-claim settlement was the first formal modern day comprehensive treaty in the province—<ref name="nisga-a-lisims_2000"/> the first signed by a [[First Nations in Canada|First Nation]] in [[British Columbia]] since the [[Douglas Treaties]] in 1854 (pertaining to areas on Vancouver Island) and [[Treaty 8]] in 1899 (pertaining to northeastern British Columbia). The agreement gives the Nisgaʼa control over their land, including the forestry and fishing resources contained in it. 

The agreement was signed on 27 May 1998 by [[Joseph Gosnell]], Nelson Leeson, and Edmond Wright of the Nisg̱a'a Nation and by Premier [[Glen Clark]] for the Province of British Columbia. Then [[Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Canada)|Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development]] [[Jane Stewart (politician)|Jane Stewart]] signed the agreement for the Canadian federal government on 4 May 1999.

==Context==
In 1887, the Nisga'a met with the then-Premier of British Columbia<ref name="Allen_Calder_40th_2014"/>{{rp|14}} to challenge the way in which the Chief Commissioner of Land and Works for the Colony of British Columbia was distributing much of Nisga'a traditional land in the Nass River valley to western settlers, in spite of the [[Royal Proclamation of 1763]], which recognized Aboriginal title in [[British North America]] and acknowledged the existence and continuity of Aboriginal self-government.<ref name="Rose_2000">{{cite book |last=Rose |first=Alex |title=Spirit Dance at Meziadin: Chief Joseph Gosnell and the Nisga'a Treaty |publisher=Harbour Publications |date=1 January 2000 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/spiritdanceatmez0000rose/page/248 248] |isbn=9781550172447 |url=https://archive.org/details/spiritdanceatmez0000rose/page/248 }}</ref>{{rp|69}}<ref name="nisga-a-lisims_FinalAgreement">{{cite web |url=http://www.nisgaalisims.ca/nisgaa-final-agreement |title=Nisga'a Final Agreement |work=Nisga'a Lisims Government |date=nd |access-date=24 October 2017 |location=[[New Aiyansh, British Columbia]] |archive-date=25 October 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171025132356/http://www.nisgaalisims.ca/nisgaa-final-agreement |url-status=dead }}</ref> By 1890, the Nisga'a Land Committee had been established.<ref name="Allen_Calder_40th_2014"/>{{rp|14}} In 1913, the Nisga'a sent a Petition to the [[Privy Council (United Kingdom)|British Privy Council]] in London requesting that their land claims be addressed by the King.<ref name="Allen_Calder_40th_2014">{{cite web |url=http://www.northernpublicaffairs.ca/index/wp-content/uploads/2014/03/Allen.pdf |title=Letter from British Columbia: reflections on the 40th anniversary of the Calder decision |first=Edward |last=Allen |date=September 2013 |work=Northern Public Affairs |pages=7|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171025184635/http://www.northernpublicaffairs.ca/index/wp-content/uploads/2014/03/Allen.pdf |archive-date=2017-10-25 }}</ref>{{rp|14}} In response, the Canadian federal government passed a law making it illegal for First Nations to "retain counsel to pursue land claims".<ref name="Allen_Calder_40th_2014"/>{{rp|14}} In 1973, [[Frank Calder (politician)|Frank Arthur Calder]] and the Nisga'a Nation Tribal Council lost the landmark case, [[Calder v British Columbia (AG)]],<ref name="Calder_1973">{{cite web|title=Calder v British Columbia (AG) |quote=Frank Calder et al., suing on their own behalf and on behalf of All Other Members of the Nishga Tribal Council, and James Gosnell et al., suing on their own behalf and on behalf of All Other Members of the Gitlakdamix Indian Band, and Maurice Nyce et al., suing on their own behalf and on behalf of All Other Members of the Canyon City Indian Band, and W.D. McKay et al., suing on their own behalf and on behalf of All Other Members of the Greenville Indian Band, and Anthony Robinson et al., suing on their own behalf and on behalf of All Other Members of the Kincolith Indian Band v. Attorney-General of British Columbia   |date=January 31, 1973  |number=[1973] S.C.R. 313 |work=Supreme Court of Canada (SCC=1970-1973)}}</ref> but the [[Supreme Court of Canada]] (SCC) ruled for the first time that [[aboriginal title]] to land existed prior to the colonization of North America. [[Thomas R. Berger|Thomas Berger]] successfully argued that the Nisga'a title to their traditional lands had never been extinguished. Calder was the first of a number of land claims negotiated in favour of the rights of aboriginal peoples.<ref name="Allen_Calder_40th_2014"/>

The 1999 Nisga'a Treaty acknowledged that "the Nisga'a people have lived in the Nass River Valley since time immemorial".<ref name="BC_laws_1999"/><ref name="nisga-a-lisims_FinalAgreement"/>

==Role of hereditary chiefs==
The Final Agreement recognized that the ''Adaawak'' (oral histories) of the hereditary chiefs ''Simgigat'' (hereditary chiefs) and ''Sigidimhaanak'' (matriarchs) continued to play an important role in accordance with the ''Ayuuk'' (Nisga'a traditional laws and practices).<ref name="BC_laws_1999">{{cite web |url=https://www.bclaws.ca/civix/document/id/lc/statreg/99002_03 |work=Province of British Columbia |title=Nisga'a Final Agreement Act: Chapter 2 - Preamble|date=1999 |access-date=24 October 2017}}</ref>

==Legal challenges==
The constitutional legality of the Nisga'a Final Agreement was challenged by some Nisga'a under [[Laxsgiik]] chief James Robinson (Sga'nisim Sim'oogit) and Mercy Thomas, particularly the self-government and law-making powers of the Nisga’a government. On 19 October 2011, the Supreme Court of British Columbia handed down its decision upholding the constitutional validity of the Nisga’a Final Agreement.
